texts: good. both predicates are kept for the night, each anchored to day 620 of Year 2 and also left in plain copular form, so "was the night warm?" and "when was it warm?" both resolve.

good. "at each lantern of the Cliff Path" becomes a fireable per-lantern rule carrying its own moth group, count and location, and the "about" hedge is kept as a spread around twenty-eight. Two cautions, neither calling for a rewrite: a hedged count lands in a slot that plain counting questions ("more than twenty?") do not currently test, and the rule produces per-lantern counts only once the corpus asserts individual lanterns belonging to the Cliff Path.
good. the crowd is typed both as a crowd and as a group of nightmoths, and the gathering stays one collective event located at the East Row.
good. same shape as the previous sentence with its own crowd witness, so the East Row and Middle Row crowds stay distinct and remain separately referable later.
good. sky-cats and cliff-spires each become a typed group keeping their genus (cat, spire), and the spires are carried as the source of the descending.
good. the sky-cats and both crowds are recognized as the ones already introduced, and the coordination becomes two hunting events, one per row, which also records where each hunt happened.

good. the hedged count, the East Row and the third watch are all carried. Note that a bare plural "Keepers" mints a fresh group of keepers each time, so these are not identified with the keepers of sentence 2; a definite "The keepers" is what would link them.
good. the Middle Row twin of the previous sentence, with its own keeper group and moth group and the same third-watch time.
good. "the next morning" resolves to day 621 of Year 2 plus the morning day-part and is ordered after the night of day 620, and the thirty-five feathers are counted on their own group.

good. "four vessels of mire-essence" is kept as a four-vessel measure on the essence (a container measure the instruction set never positively licenses, but nothing is lost), and "that day" resolves to day 621, the day of the feather collecting — if the night of day 620 was meant, date the sentence explicitly.
